title: How deep is your network? Deep vs. shallow learning of transfer operators
claim: A cheap randomized-feature method matches the spectral estimates of an expensive deep-learning baseline and the exact solution.
layout: 3 panels in a row; eigenvalues, eigenfunctions, error by dimension; shared legends
description: A single row of three matplotlib-style scatter and line plots, labeled (a), (b) and (c) in bold above each panel. Panel (a) plots the four leading eigenvalues λ_i against index i. Blue dots for RaNNDy, orange crosses for VAMPnets and green stars for the exact values sit on top of each other, so the methods look identical. Panel (b) plots three eigenfunctions φ1 (red), φ2 (green) and φ3 (blue) over x from -2 to 2. Solid lines are RaNNDy, dashed lines VAMPnets and dotted lines the exact solution, and all three nearly overlap. Panel (c) shows relative error against dimension (2, 3, 4) for VAMPnet (blue dots) and RaNNDy (orange stars). Both stay near 0.02, with RaNNDy slightly higher. Gridlines and small in-plot legends are the only decoration.
caption: OU process results. (a) Four dominant eigenvalues showing a perfect match between RaNNDy, VAMPnets, and the exact eigenvalues. (b) Three dominant eigenfuntions. The solid lines represent RaNNDy approximations, dashed lines are VAMPnets, and dotted lines are the exact eigenfunctions. (c) Comparison of approximation errors for multi-dimensional OU processes.
abstract: We introduce RaNNDy, a randomized neural network framework for learning transfer operators and their spectral decompositions. By fixing the weights of the hidden layers and training only the output layer, RaNNDy achieves significant reductions in computational costs -- often by two orders of magnitude -- with similar accuracy compared to state-of-the-art deep learning methods. The method is less sensitive to hyperparameter tuning and provides a closed-form solution for the output layer weights that directly represent eigenfunctions of the learned operator. Moreover, it is possible to estimate uncertainties associated with the computed spectral properties via ensemble learning. We demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed approach using diverse benchmark problems, including stochastic dynamical systems and protein folding processes, highlighting the strengths but also weaknesses of RaNNDy.
